comment_text: I kinda noticed something in the thumbnail with the two images. Yes one may be more flashy and one could even say “looks better”, but comparing the two I think gets to the heart of what art is.  Look at the two faces. One is a blank stare. Nice to look at but there’s nothing in those eyes. One has a very decisive emotion behind it that is easy to relate to.  Art is not about creating beautiful things. Art often does result in beautiful things though because of what it actually is. It’s a means of human connection. It’s a form of communication between ourselves to display visceral ideas that we ourselves can’t be put any other way.  If art simply was just a means of creating “good images”, then yeah, sure. AI has “solved” art. We don’t need it anymore.  AI may be able to recreate the “ghibli style” or make hyper realistic images or have incredible shading, but it can’t conceive and invent something like Picasso’s Guernica, or the emotional weight of something like a Rothko painting. AI couldn’t think of signing a toilet and calling it art.  Dare I say, AI couldn’t think of something like taping a banana to a wall with duct tape.  Why?  Because these statements are windows into the minds of their creator.  Humans depend on connection. We need each other. Left on our own, we can not survive. We’re social creatures, introverted as some of us are. Art is a means of true human connection.  An AI could maybe write a really catchy melody. Four AI bots, however, couldn’t hang around each other in Liverpool, dreaming up romantic songs about their young lives in the 60s and express their joy to the world in the way they did. An AI might be able to write some surreal imagery and put it to an acoustic guitar. But it can’t pull together the experience and the single creative vision behind something by Bob Dylan. Heck, AI could ABSOLUTELY randomize white noise for 2 hours. But it can’t do it with the intentionality and the natural, human ebbing and flowing of someone like Merzbow. It can take a bunch of old records and maybe sorta cobble it together into an audio piece about dementia. But it couldn’t have the human heartbreak and empathy to create something like those final few minutes of The Caretaker’s EATEOT (which I think I’ve only heard 2 seconds of… but oh man, those 2 seconds…).  AI could end a cartoon episode about a fear of the outdoors in a silly way. But it takes a uniquely strange and funny group of people to end it with a guy in a gorilla suit literally smacking a wooden chair wwe style into an animated starfish and squirrel SUPPOSEDLY “in a bag” and then immediately stop when the talking sponge asks what the heck it’s doing underwater with a reveal that a family was watching the episode on TV in utter bewilderment.  It’s why when you talking about reading someone’s books or poems, you often refer to them as reading T.S. Elliott. You’re reading Dickinson. You’re reading Kafka. You’re reading Tolkien. You’re reading THEM. That’s what you’re there to read. Not in a parasocial way (hopefully), but in a way that you emotionally engage with their thoughts. You’re not there for the book itself: the collection of words in and of themselves.  AI, in this instance, only knows how to write the book.
